Let  
\[
c=\sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i\beta_i,\qquad a^2=\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i^2,\qquad b^2=\sum_{i=1}^n\beta_i^2.
\]
Then \(a,b<1\) and by Cauchy–Schwarz \(|c|\le ab\). Also
\[
A^2B^2=(1-a^2)(1-b^2),\qquad 2W=(1-c)^2.
\]
We first show
\[
A^2B^2\le 2W.
\]
If \(c\le 0\), then \((1-c)^2\ge 1\ge (1-a^2)(1-b^2)\).  
If \(c>0\), then \(c\le ab\), so
\[
(1-c)^2\ge (1-ab)^2,
\]
and
\[
(1-ab)^2-(1-a^2)(1-b^2)=(a-b)^2\ge0.
\]
Thus \(A^2B^2\le (1-ab)^2\le (1-c)^2=2W\).

Now assume \(\lambda\ne0\) and all roots are real. Let \(e_k\) be the elementary symmetric sums of the roots. For
\[
P(x)=x^n+\lambda x^{n-1}+\cdots+\lambda x^3+\lambda Wx^2+\lambda ABx+\lambda,
\]
we have
\[
e_{n-1}=(-1)^{n-1}\lambda AB,\quad
e_{n-2}=(-1)^{n-2}\lambda W,\quad
e_n=(-1)^n\lambda.
\]
Newton’s inequality for \(k=n-1\) gives
\[
\left(\frac{e_{n-1}}{n}\right)^2
\ge
\left(\frac{e_{n-2}}{\binom n2}\right)e_n.
\]
Substituting,
\[
\frac{\lambda^2 A^2B^2}{n^2}
\ge
\frac{\lambda^2 W}{\binom n2}.
\]
Since \(\lambda\ne0\),
\[
A^2B^2\ge \frac{n^2}{\binom n2}W
=\frac{2n}{n-1}W.
\]
But \(\frac{2n}{n-1}>2\), so \(A^2B^2>2W\), contradicting \(A^2B^2\le2W\).

Therefore no nonzero \(\lambda\) works. If \(\lambda=0\), the polynomial is \(x^n=0\), whose roots are all real.

\[
\boxed{\lambda=0}
\]
